look_here_first: Start with the very small CUP/RING at an individual spikelet's base, and a DENSE HAIR RING for the true leaf ligule. The existing photo shows visible spikelets and axis but NOT the tiny cup or leaf collar: inspect a macro before confirming.

best_field_traits: Native Texas perennial bunch grass; commonly ~0.3–1.2 m high, not rhizomatous.
Soft rather lax leaf blades; lower sheaths may be hairy.
True ligule is dense ring of straight hairs.
Inflorescence narrow with appressed short racemes and fuzzy green spikelets.
Tiny cuplike ring at the base of a mature spikelet just above its pedicel. Requires high magnification.
After dispersal, residual zigzag branch axis may remain.
crew_field_check: Check rooted perennial tuft; see whether aboveground creeping stems are absent.
Pull open a true blade/sheath collar and look for dense straight hair ligule, not just nearby leaf hairs.
At 10–20× compare one individual mature spikelet base for the tiny cup/ring structure.
Don't conclude E. sericea from one head photo where the cup/ligule can't be seen.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: 1–2 mm-scale macro of cup- or ring-like structure directly below a mature spikelet with its pedicel attached.
Side-by-side one-flower-head view plus individual spikelet showing soft silky hairs and pedicel hairs.
Clear 10× view of true DENSE HAIR LIGULE at collar, distinct from sheath or blade hairs.
Whole rooted robust bunch with site habitat and ruler; seedhead after spikelets detach (zigzag remnant).

comparisons.key_distinctions: E. sericea — tufted perennial commonly about 0.3–1.2 m; soft blades, ring of straight ligular hairs, small fuzzy clustered spikelets on short hair-bearing stalks; tiny cup at spikelet base. Paspalum spp. — can have spikelets in one-sided racemes but lack the diagnostic Eriochloa cup-like lower attachment; their ligule is generally membranous rather than a dense hair ring. Digitaria spp. — often spreading grasses with fingerlike racemes and paired spikelets; no Eriochloa cup at each spikelet base. Inspect the same-plant base and spikelet attachments. Panicum spp. — open or contracted panicles, but do not share the cup-like spikelet base; check spikelet, stalk, ligule with magnification.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · FIND THE BUNCH
field_id_short_tiles.cue: Erect robust perennial tuft, usually 0.3–1.2 m
field_id_short_tiles.expand: Photograph the rooted crown and lower sheaths. Texas cupgrass is caespitose (tufted) and lacks long rhizomes. Other bunchgrasses can mimic habit, so crown alone is not proof. A separate exact-source live tuft photo now appears in the gallery; only green blades and upright culms are actually arrowed, not buried roots.
field_id_short_tiles.photo_status: IN-GROUND LIVE TUFT PHOTOGRAPHED; UNDERGROUND ROOTS NOT EXPOSED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.cue: Ligule = tight fringe of straight hairs, not a membrane
field_id_short_tiles.expand: Fold the blade aside and magnify the actual inner blade/sheath junction at 10–20×. Hairs on leaf margins, sheath or nodes are NOT the true ligule. The available Noble grass-photo reference is study-only until rights are verified.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · FOLLOW THE FLOWER HEAD
field_id_short_tiles.cue: Narrow central axis with 4–10 short, erect, one-sided side racemes
field_id_short_tiles.expand: Kew describes the individual racemes as about 1.5–3 cm and the spikelets in two rows, on hairy short pedicels. Three real source-credited photos show broad green and dry flowering-head outlines. Current markers indicate gross axis and lateral units, NOT the tiny cup.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · PROVE THE CUP
field_id_short_tiles.cue: Single 3.6–4.2 mm spikelet has a globular callus / cup at its base
field_id_short_tiles.expand: A credited Bob Harms source-labelled image shows the pale globular cup/callus at the base of a DETACHED spikelet and contains a source scale. One marker indicates the visible cup. The attachment to a hairy pedicel is still NOT documented; obtain a 1-mm-scaled connected specimen to finish this character.
field_id_short_tiles.photo_status: DETACHED BASAL CUP PHOTOGRAPHED; ATTACHED PEDICEL + SCALE VALIDATION MISSING
field_id_short_tiles.certainty: DETACHED CUP PHOTO SUPPORTED / ATTACHMENT HOLD

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · OPEN A MATURE SPIKELET
field_id_short_tiles.cue: Lower glume obscure/adnate; upper glume and sterile lemma are each five-veined
field_id_short_tiles.expand: Kew GrassBase: the 3.6–4.2 mm spikelet has a basal sterile floret and one fertile floret. The LOWER GLUME is absent as a free obvious bract or extremely reduced/adnate into the globular callus; do not draw an invented separate lower glume. The pubescent membranous UPPER GLUME is about as long as the spikelet and five-veined. The lower sterile lemma is likewise about spikelet-length and five-veined; its palea is insignificant. Photograph an intact spikelet plus the separated upper glume and sterile lemma on a 1-mm scale before any fine arrows.
field_id_short_tiles.photo_status: PUBLISHED REPRODUCTIVE ANATOMY — OPENED SPIKELET PHOTO MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · FIND THE HARD FERTILE LEMMA
field_id_short_tiles.cue: Hard ~3-mm fertile lemma with minute ~0.3–0.5-mm awn; compare cupgrass look-alikes
field_id_short_tiles.expand: Kew describes the fertile lemma as about 3 mm, hardened (indurate), finely wrinkled (rugulose), with inward-rolled margins and a tiny terminal point/awn about 0.3–0.5 mm. It is NOT a long projecting awn. Compare Paspalum and Digitaria using a mature spikelet BASE: Eriochloa has the globular callus/cup and a true ligule of hairs; the others do not share that precise cup structure. Do not transfer generic Paspalum/Digitaria ligule claims to every species. The detached cup photo is useful, but attached pedicel, separated lemma and calibrated ligule remain unproved.
field_id_short_tiles.photo_status: DETACHED CUP SUPPORTED; FERTILE LEMMA AND MATCHED LOOK-ALIKES MISSING

field_photo_quickcheck.title: TEXAS CUPGRASS — 20-second first look; confirm tiny anatomy with lens
photo_sequence: Living in-ground leafy bunch — 2026-10-27 reused archived Theresa Strickler CC BY photograph, roots not excavated
steps: 1. BUNCH: new gallery panel 5 shows ACTUAL source-identified in-ground leafy tuft among dry litter with upright green culms. Roots are not exposed, nor is a same-root entire flowering plant independently traceable. Do not arrow underground anatomy.
2. LIGULE: gently spread TRUE inner blade/sheath junction. Dense straight hair fringe, not smooth membrane. A nearby hairy node or sheath edge is NOT the ligule. Decisive macro currently MISSING.
3. HEAD: several short narrowly ascending one-sided racemes crowded along a hairy main axis. Kew GrassBase: 4–10 racemes, 1.5–3 cm each; 3.6–4.2-mm individual spikelets.

4. CUP: at 10–20× follow an intact fuzzy spikelet DOWN onto its short hairy pedicel to the globular basal callus/cup. An archived Bob Harms photo ALREADY shows the pale cup beneath a DETACHED spikelet; that is genuine cup evidence, but the intact attachment to its hairy pedicel is STILL MISSING. Do not infer that attachment or cup dimensions from the detached view.

5. CHECK native look-alikes in genus: Paspalum or Digitaria often have membranous rather than dense-hair-fringe true ligules and no Eriochloa basal cup; never remove native grass on head appearance alone.

6. Take FOUR linked photos from the same identified plant: tuft/crown, full panicle, opened collar with millimeter scale, and intact spikelet–pedicel cup with millimeter scale. Without macro, mark probable Eriochloa / hold species.

7. NEW PHOTO 4 ACTUAL CUP: Bob Harms original ERSE5-9 depicts the small PALE GLOBULAR CUP/CALLUS beneath a detached Texas cupgrass spikelet; photo arrows target the pale base and spikelet above it. This is not a fully attached pedicel, nor a 1-mm measure, nor true hair ligule.
field_photo_quickcheck.photo_caveat: Archived Bob Harms source photo demonstrates a pale globular basal cup on DETACHED E. sericea spikelets, with a visible cup arrow; the connected spikelet–hairy-pedicel insertion and its calibrated measurement remain unphotographed.
